FREEDOM AS A STATE OF META-HAIRESIS
(Purposiveness, the Horizon of the Possible, and the Measure of Freedom. A First Approximation)

For years, a person could not break free from addiction. They knew everything about the harm, the danger, the catastrophic consequences, and what they thought was the only thing that could save them: “I must never do it again.” Knowing did not help. Each new situation, however different, led to the same outcome in a closed cycle of addiction that tightened relentlessly.
Yet some time after successful psychotherapy, the same person says, “The thought sometimes comes back. But right on its heels comes another: ‘I don’t need it anymore.’”

Consider that phrase. The person does not say, “I mustn’t.” They describe no struggle between desire and prohibition and make no choice between using and abstaining. The choice itself seems to have vanished because the field of possibilities in which it once arose has changed.
What happened to this person’s freedom? Did it diminish because one possibility no longer held any appeal? Or did it expand because many other ways forward opened up where there had been only one?

The usual understanding of freedom cannot answer this question. Freedom is usually understood as the ability to choose among possible courses of action, and many contemporary debates revolve around this view. A person is considered free if they can choose among several options. If prior causes or external coercion fully determine that choice, their freedom seems limited or even impossible.

There is a problem hidden in this view. The act of choosing is already an action of a kind, and thus an event within the causal order. Neuropsychological experiments, showing that an action is selected in the brain’s neural structures several hundred milliseconds (in some later studies, even seconds) before it reaches awareness, all concern the act of choosing, which is itself an action. If prior causes fully determine the choice, it is determined. If they do not, a different difficulty arises. How do we distinguish freedom from chance?
Perhaps this dilemma arises because we are looking for freedom in the wrong place. The person who says “I don’t need it” suggests where to look instead, in what precedes the act of choosing.

I propose that we consider freedom a distinct state in which a horizon opens and is held open for the formation of a new image of reality. A choice may come later, once the possible directions begin to take more definite shape.
In other words, freedom does not choose among possibilities. It precedes the choice among them.

This thesis grows out of the concept of purposiveness that I proposed in “Purposiveness as Vector of Information: From Bits to a New Image of Reality” and “Purposiveness as a Vector of the Optimal Expansion of the Image of Reality” [1, 2]. In those essays I linked purposiveness to reality’s capacity to form a new image of itself, particularly in cognition and the formation of meaning.

Here I explore a broader, ontological reading of that thesis. If we take it as a working hypothesis, a question arises. Can reality be in a state in which a new image has yet to become actual, while the horizon for its formation has already opened?

This essay is a first approximation rather than a finished theory. I will therefore sketch out certain questions and leave them open. Even at this stage, the approach allows us to see freedom differently and ask both whether it is present and to what degree.
Since this article introduces several new terms, I will set them out at the start. Each is explained in more detail and illustrated where it comes up in the argument.
Purposiveness is reality’s inherent capacity to form a new image of itself. The term refers to the capacity to form a new whole, rather than to an external goal or predetermined outcome.

A new image of reality is a new whole in which the form and mode of existence of reality enter into a new relationship. It is reality itself that is transformed. In cognition, as I have suggested before, a new image may also find expression in meaning and in concepts [3].

Meta-hairesis is a local, liminal state above and beyond choice. Several possible directions in which reality or a local system could unfold are held open together, without any one of them immediately becoming the actual continuation.

Neusis-horizon is the structured horizon of co-present possible directions in which a new image of reality can take shape. It concerns directions before they take the form of a list or range of options for choice.
Aperture boundary is the boundary at which a system’s causal history continues to operate even as a horizon of structurally available continuations opens up for this system.
Presencing of the possible is the presence, in a system’s current state, of structural relations that allow for several as yet unrealised continuations.
Redundant stability is a state in which events and experiences change while the system reproduces the same mode of existence.

Causal vortex is a pattern of repetition in which the effects recreate the conditions for the same trajectory, and the horizon of the possible steadily narrows. It is a spiral in which the effects reproduce their cause, which in turn brings about the same effects, and the process continues to spiral inward.

Open spiral is a pattern of repetition in which a recognisable element of prior experience enters a new configuration of connections, opening up other ways forward. On the next “turn” of this spiral, earlier causes may lead to a different continuation as reality unfolds.
2. The Historical Horizon. From Freedom of Choice to Freedom as Openness
The history of philosophy offers many answers to the question of freedom. Those that allow us to distinguish freedom from the act of choosing are especially relevant here.

As early as the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle discusses prohairesis, a considered choice distinct from simple desire or immediate impulse [4]. For Aristotle, choice is the outcome of a process that takes place before the action is performed. He does not yet consider that process a distinct ontological state of freedom.

In considering liberum arbitrium, Augustine links freedom of the will to the moral responsibility of a person capable of choosing between good and evil [5]. Ever since, the relationship between freedom, will, and responsibility has been a central question in Western philosophy.

Spinoza takes a fundamentally different position. He calls free that which acts from the necessity of its own nature. A person believes themselves free because they are conscious of their desires but unaware of the causes that determine them [6]. For Spinoza, freedom is compatible with necessity and operates within it.

In the Third Antinomy of the Critique of Pure Reason, Kant sets natural causality against the possibility of spontaneously beginning a causal series [7]. This makes the problem particularly acute. If freedom is the beginning of a new causal sequence, how can that be beginning something other than a continuation of prior necessity or a matter of chance?

With Schelling, the problem of freedom takes on a broader ontological significance. His philosophy allows us to think of nature as a productive process in which things come into being, beyond the familiar picture of a collection of things already formed. In his 1809 treatise, he relates freedom to the deep grounds of human existence and to the real possibility of good and evil [8]. What particularly concerns us here is the idea that the formation of something new is a property of reality itself.

Bergson criticises the conception of a free act as a choice among ready-made alternatives. On his view, that picture distorts the lived duration of mental life by turning it into a spatial scheme. A free action grows out of the personality as a whole, beyond any comparison of possible decisions [9]. The patient with whom we began might agree. Their newfound “I don’t need it” did not come from comparing alternatives.

For Jaspers, freedom is bound up with the existential experience of boundary situations, in which familiar ways of living reveal their inadequacy [10]. His boundary situation differs from the state I will call meta-hairesis, but his idea that a boundary can reveal something about human existence matters to us.

Heidegger approaches freedom through Seinlassen, letting beings be and remaining open to their disclosure [11]. Freedom here is a particular way of relating to what discloses itself, a departure from the idea that it consists in having ready-made alternatives at one’s disposal.

Sartre, by contrast, puts choice back at the centre of human existence. Human beings cannot escape the necessity of defining themselves through their own actions. His account thus stands in marked contrast to the understanding of freedom proposed here [12].

Whitehead may come closest to our concerns. In his process philosophy, reality comes about through the becoming of actual occasions in which the many enter into a new unity. What we encounter as finished things takes shape in these processes. Creativity is a fundamental category of this becoming [13].

Isaiah Berlin’s distinction between negative and positive liberty, together with Amartya Sen’s account of what people are actually able to do and be (capabilities), lets us ask how far freedom depends on the field of possibilities available to a person, beyond the formal absence of coercion [14, 15].

These accounts each give us a different way to ask about freedom beyond its simple identification with the act of choosing. They belong to distinct philosophical projects, and their relevance to the definition proposed here is indirect.
I propose taking a further step and considering freedom a distinct state of openness to the possible that arises at the boundary where a new image of reality begins to form.
3. Purposiveness and the Problem of Causal Continuity

In earlier work, I proposed understanding purposiveness as reality’s property or capacity of forming a new image of itself [1, 2]. I retain that definition here, but the term “image” needs a more precise meaning.

As I understand it, purposiveness means that the reality already in existence can bring forth something new while remaining connected to what it has been. This can occur without a fixed goal, an external design, or a future state directing the present. The idea seems intuitive when we consider living beings that continue themselves in their offspring, or a culture that constantly reproduces itself through transformations and innovations. To extend purposiveness to reality as a whole, as such, requires an argument of its own, which I have partly developed in earlier work.

All our experience suggests that no new image of reality arises ex nihilo. It arises in relation to what already exists, even when it involves a radical reorganisation or the destruction of the previous organisation. Yet for a change to count as the formation of a new image, continuity between the previous and subsequent images of reality is insufficient on its own.

A causal account explains the course and conditions of reality’s continual, interconnected transformation. Purposiveness poses a different question. Under what conditions does a transformation form a new image, a new whole within reality? Both explanatory questions can be asked within the causal order, without positing a separate physical force or agency. If only because a change in a single parameter does not always give rise to a new image.

A rock slowly worn away and altered by erosion may remain the same whole, the same rock, in a succession of different states. A stone that breaks away may become a separate object while retaining essentially the same mode of existence.
I therefore propose to understand a new image as a new whole in which the form and mode of existence of reality enter into a new relationship.

Novelty here concerns a new organisation of the structural relations of an object, or even of reality as a whole, together with the possibilities for further existence that this organisation opens up. The magnitude of a change or the mere appearance of a separate object is insufficient to establish novelty.

A child, for example, is a new individual whole in whom what is inherited finds a unique expression, without giving rise to a new biological form of the species. In cognition, the emergence of a new image may alter the overall relation between the knower and what is known while leaving the object of cognition intact. At these levels, the concept of an “image” retains its force and can signify more than a subjective reflection.
This is the fundamental distinction between a change of state and the formation of a new image.

Purposiveness cannot be identified with mere change, with destruction, or with simple self-preservation. Any one of them can occur without a new whole taking shape, or it may provide a condition for its formation at another level of organisation.

A system may continue to exist, temporarily preserve its present state, or even cease to exist. These three outcomes - continuation, preservation (stagnation), and cessation (destruction) – are insufficient in themselves as criteria of purposiveness. There are good reasons to think that the loss of an individual element can sometimes support the reorganisation of a larger system. In living systems, for example, the death of certain cells (as in apoptosis¹ [16]) serves the further development of the organism as a whole.

Preservation can likewise create the conditions for a further transformation or simply reproduce what was there before. We must therefore keep in mind which whole and which timescale we are considering.

If we adopt this definition of purposiveness and turn to the question of freedom, we must ask which directions of further formation a system has available to it, how they become available, and whether the system can hold them open “without making any decision for the time being.”

Causality continues to operate as a system approaches the boundary of its prior organisation. The system’s history may prepare and even bring about this boundary. At the boundary, however, the continuation customary to the system may lose its predominance. At the same time, other directions in which the system could unfold may open up and become available.
Strict determinism asks whether the complete prior state uniquely determines the subsequent course of events.

This article pursues a different question. Which possible continuations are available to a particular system as it interacts with its environment, and how does their availability change? To pursue this question, we can bracket strict determinism for the time being.

The availability of possible continuations, or the system’s openness, must be effective at the level at which we are considering the system and in relation to the purposiveness of its continued existence. A direction in which the system can unfold is structurally available, within definite constraints, if its existing capacities and relations allow that direction to develop. Changes in the system’s capacities and relations can in turn alter the very horizon of the possible.
4. Meta-Hairesis. A State Above and Beyond Choice

Imagine someone who, through war, illness, or some other serious circumstance, has lost the profession that defined their life for decades. Many know the moment when the old way forward has lost its force and a new one has yet to take shape. The person has made no decision. They are in a state “above and beyond choice” and see no clear options. Yet they sense that something is opening up. Certain directions begin to come into view, although none has yet taken the form of a decision.
I propose the term meta-hairesis for this state.
The term derives from the Greek αἵρεσις (hairesis), “choice” or “selection,” and meta-, which here has the specific sense of going above and beyond the act of choosing.

Meta-hairesis is a state above and beyond choice as such, distinct from making another choice among possibilities. The system remains connected to its causal history and has entered a liminal state in which it holds open several structurally available directions for its continued existence at once.

The system’s causal history, of course, explains how this configuration at the boundary arose and continues to operate within it. Meta-hairesis concerns a different feature of the system. Given this configuration at the boundary, what continuations of its prior history now open up?

This is the sense in which a liminal state differs from an intermediate one. An intermediate state implies movement or interaction between states whose outlines are already clear. A liminal state describes a situation in which the prior organisation continues to operate even as other directions begin to become available. The future form of reality is still taking shape and has yet to become actual.

The intuition behind this idea comes from an experience familiar to us all. We know the moment when something in the mind is already “knocking at the door” but cannot yet be put into words. We seem to have caught an idea and yet cannot formulate it. Or we “know” that we have something important to say and do not yet know what it is.

An optical aperture offers a metaphor for this state. The aperture² is distinct from the place where the image appears. It sets the conditions for the passage of light, determining which rays get through and how much light reaches the other side. This determines which images can form at all. The analogy concerns the boundary itself and the constraints it imposes; it does not imply that optical and ontological processes are conceptually identical.

In our account, the aperture boundary is the boundary at which the prior causal history still operates as a condition and a constraint, yet that history no longer exhausts the horizon of possible continuations. The aperture itself makes no choice. It makes possible the formation of an image. Likewise, freedom in the state of meta-hairesis involves no prescribed or offered choice. It designates a liminal state of openness in which a new image can take shape.
In this sense, freedom as meta-hairesis can be understood as a local state of openness at an aperture boundary.
5. The Neusis-Horizon³. A Horizon of Possible Directions
If meta-hairesis names a state, we need a different concept for the structure of what becomes possible in that state. I propose calling it the neusis-horizon.

The Greek νεῦσις (neusis) is associated with inclination, leaning, or direction. In ancient Greek geometry, neusis also referred to a particular kind of construction or problem-solving that went beyond the constraints of using only a compass and straightedge. This historical parallel is chiefly a metaphor, but it brings out a feature of the concept. The neusis-horizon extends beyond a given set of possibilities already afforded by the tools at hand.

The neusis-horizon is a structured horizon of possible directions in which a new image of reality can take shape. It extends beyond any list of ready-made alternatives from which a system might choose.
The distinction between a direction and an option matters here. An option is a possibility that has already taken sufficient shape to be compared with another.
A direction, by contrast, is a possible way for something to take shape. A specific option may or may not emerge from it.

Let us return to the person who lost their profession. A direction might be something like “building a life on what I can do with my hands”. Specific options would take shape later: opening a workshop, teaching the craft, or going into restoration. The direction precedes and gives rise to the options. Without it, those options would never have come into view.
In a state of freedom, directions open up. Choice concerns more clearly defined options for action. The neusis-horizon is therefore open and structurally constrained at the same time.
It is open because it may encompass several co-present directions, none of which has yet been actualised.
It is constrained because the system’s history, structure, and interaction with its environment limit the continuations available to it.
Someone who has worked with their hands all their life is unlikely to discover a sudden inclination towards theoretical physics, although even that cannot be ruled out entirely.

The point is not an unlimited possibility of anything whatsoever, but a plurality of structurally admissible directions. To assess this openness, we need to ask what in the system’s organisation and its interaction with its environment makes each direction available. Structural availability concerns what the system can bring about, and how. This brings us back to a central question. What does a system need in order to hold directions open, rather than merely undergo change?

Our account looks for an answer in the postulated principle of purposiveness, according to which any system, and even reality as a whole, has the capacity to form a new image of itself. In the case of a person, or indeed any living system, Karl Friston’s mathematically formulated Free Energy Principle accounts for a similar capacity in terms of an internal generative “model of the world,” through which living systems can maintain their organisation and anticipate sensory states and ways of interacting with their environment [17–19].

Whether such formal modelling can be identified with the presencing of the possible in the ontological sense proposed here, that is, with respect to reality as a whole, remains an open question. A stone, as we shall see, has no such internal representation.
6. The Presencing⁴ of the Possible and the Problem of Novelty
We have arrived at a more difficult question. How can something that is yet to become actual belong in some way to the present state of reality?

Let us return to the previous example. Anyone who has undertaken creative work or research knows the feeling that a solution is “somewhere close” even though they have yet to find it. It is still elusive, yet somehow already present. We can recognise wrong answers as wrong while still lacking the right answer that would let us say why. How, then, can we recognise what is wrong when we do not yet know the right answer?
I propose the concept of the presencing of the possible to describe this circumstance.

In its present state, the system has structural relations that allow for several as yet unrealised continuations. This does not mean that the future image already exists somewhere, hidden and ready-made. In other words, the system is poised to realise itself in one of several continuations that are present on its horizon at the same time.

Where, then, do the available directions come from? And where do the optimally purposive directions among them come from, those in which a new image of the system can take shape for the system itself? Some open up through capacities it already has. Others may require a reorganisation of its internal and external relations.

In meta-hairesis, the horizon can hold available directions open, as in the example of creative work. Under certain conditions, the neusis-horizon itself may also be reshaped. Processes within the system may establish new configurations of relations that make previously unavailable directions structurally available.

The system’s future state and the horizon of what could become possible for it both change. A horizon in which previously inaccessible possibilities become available differs from the one within which the system had been unfolding along familiar lines. New, optimally purposive possibilities may open up within this horizon and take shape as a new image, a new whole.

We must then ask whether this expansion of the horizon simply reveals what was hidden or brings a genuinely new and purposive possibility into being. Our inability to describe the new in advance in terms of what preceded it still leaves open the question of whether its possibility already belonged to reality and simply went unrecognised.

The question remains unresolved. Yet it lets us formulate one of the account’s central hypotheses. Freedom may concern the possibility of reshaping the very horizon of the future as well as the openness of the future itself.
7. The Measure of Freedom. Breadth, Durability, and the Reshaping of the Horizon
If freedom is a state of meta-hairesis, a further question inevitably arises. Is every such state equally free?

Probably not. The structured openness of the possible can vary in its configuration, how long it lasts, and its capacity to be reshaped. Freedom can therefore be considered a state that admits of degrees.

The measure of freedom cannot be identified with the number of available options. This is not only a matter of measurement: from the outset we have located freedom above and beyond the act of choosing.

Imagine someone with dozens of almost identical possibilities ahead of them: thirty similar jobs in the same field or thirty apartments in the same neighbourhood. Consider someone else who has only two directions open to them, but these are fundamentally different. They can stay and rebuild their life here, or start afresh somewhere else. The first person has many more options, but they differ very little from one another. The second person is, so to speak, on the verge of a bifurcation in their life trajectory. The first person’s greater number of options does not in itself mean a broader horizon of freedom.

The first dimension of freedom can therefore be understood as the breadth of the neusis-horizon, the degree of structural diversity among the directions available at the aperture boundary. Counting those directions alone tells us little about their diversity.

The second dimension is the durability of the neusis-horizon’s openness. The horizon of the possible may remain open for only a moment or be held open for a long time without settling into one actual continuation. Long-term psychoanalytic therapy can offer an illustration. Analysands may spend a long time in a state in which “nothing changes,” then quickly and perceptibly form a new, constructive position in life. To paraphrase Thomas Ogden, one of today’s leading psychoanalysts, psychoanalysis itself takes no more than a week or two, but the therapy has to be sustained for years before then, even when it seems as though nothing is happening (as relayed by one of his supervisees, 2026).

Duration alone, however, does not guarantee greater freedom. The ability to hold possibilities open differs from indecision, stagnation, or an inability to move into a new state. Someone who has “yet to decide” after years is not necessarily freer than someone who decided quickly. Durability means that openness remains effective. Over time, the directions do not fade but grow more distinct.

A third characteristic may be the capacity to reshape the very horizon of the possible. Can a system, in the course of its own existence, create a “field” in which new directions can emerge, as well as hold open those it already has available?
This third characteristic is particularly conjectural. Yet it may be decisive in distinguishing freedom as a state of openness from freedom as a condition for giving form to something new.
We can thus provisionally describe the measure of freedom in three respects.
Breadth of the horizon concerns the diversity of structurally available directions.
Durability of the horizon concerns how long the system can keep those directions effectively open.
Capacity to reshape the horizon concerns how far the horizon itself can change as a new image takes shape.

These characteristics need not reduce to a single numerical formula. Formalising them would be a separate task, requiring a definition of the system’s state space, the relevant timescales, and the criteria for structural novelty. Even asking how freedom admits of degrees, however, allows us to reconsider several of its longstanding paradoxes.
A) Can a Stone Be Free?
Let us begin with the simplest and at the same time the most awkward example.

If purposiveness, in the sense proposed here, is a universal capacity of reality, a stone participates in the processes through which reality changes itself. The question of whether an individual stone generates a new image, let alone whether it is in a state of freedom, remains separate.

A stone can crumble, heat up, shift, or split. Deformation alone does not amount to a new image in which form and mode of existence constitute a new whole. When the stone becomes part of an arch, however, the relations take on a new organisation, and the whole acquires new properties. That novelty belongs to the arch as a structure, not to the stone taken in isolation.

This example shows why we need to distinguish the individual object, the larger whole, and the process of their transformation. The purposiveness of a transformation at the larger scale does not confer freedom on each of its components.

A simple macroscopic model describes the stone’s motion given certain initial conditions. Changing those conditions gives a different trajectory. Even a chance deviation from the trajectory does not make the stone free. The stone has nothing that could hold directions open and no possible continuations of its own in the sense discussed in Section 5.

The stone thus tests two distinctions at once, the distinction between a change and a new image, and the distinction between the possibility of a new image and freedom. Our account accommodates this case without ascribing freedom to the stone itself.
The prisoner poses a different problem.

Someone deprived of physical freedom may have an extremely narrow horizon for action in the world. Imprisonment constrains their movements, social contacts, and practical opportunities. Their psychic life and the meanings they can form may remain open to a different degree.

A person may retain the ability to think, reinterpret experience, imagine the future, form new conceptual relations, and develop a different image of themselves. The experience of Epictetus, who endured slavery (as, according to ancient accounts, did Plato and Aesop), and the creative work of Taras Shevchenko in exile remind us that external constraint and the possibility of inward transformation do not necessarily coincide.

Freedom therefore cannot be expressed as a single measure for “the human being in general.” It depends on the level of organisation at which we consider the neusis-horizon. A prisoner’s opportunities for physical action may be almost entirely closed, while the scope for changes in their inner life and in what gives it meaning may remain much wider. A person may be constrained in one respect and retain considerable openness in another.

Conversely, a person free from external coercion may remain so confined to familiar ways of perceiving and acting that they discover virtually no new directions for their own life. They may consider their existence quite satisfactory and even purposive in its own way, although their horizon of the possible is almost closed and their life has stagnated. The formal absence of coercion offers no guarantee of a broad horizon of freedom. A reworded everyday maxim makes the point with bitter irony: “Eat your fill and sleep your fill, and God will send you happiness still.” Here happiness is not made but awaited. The entire neusis-horizon fits between the plate and the pillow.

The opposite of freedom is thus not exhausted by external coercion; on our account, it can also be found in the narrowing or closing of the horizon of the possible. Coercion matters in its own right. As imprisonment shows, it can place real limits on how a person’s possibilities can be actualised. Inner openness can never justify depriving someone of freedom from without.
C) Addiction. The Causal Vortex and the Open Spiral
Let us return to the person with whom we began. Their case shows something neither the stone nor the prisoner can show: how a horizon can narrow from within, without any “walls.”

In my account of addiction [20], the addictive agent sets off a chain of effects that become the cause of repeated recourse to the same agent. Using a substance or gambling brings brief relief or gratification. The discomfort that follows and the desire to experience relief again sustain the repetition. This is how redundant stability⁵ arises. Events and experiences change, while the same mode of existence steadily reproduces itself in a spiral.

I call this a causal vortex when the effects of each turn of the loop deepen dependence on a self-reproducing causal trajectory. A cause produces an effect, the effect renews the same cause, which brings about the same effect again, and so on. More and more of life’s situations have the same continuation, while other directions cease to be available. The loop becomes a spiral that steadily narrows into a vortex. As it deepens, important relationships and ways of living may break down. In this sense the vortex is a process of anti-freedom, as the neusis-horizon contracts to a single point.

In follow-up interviews after transfigurative psychotherapy [20] patients described a different sequence. The thought of using a substance or gambling sometimes returns, but it is followed almost at once by “I really don’t need it.” They say the urge to use or gamble again does not arise. I describe this change as a passage from “I mustn’t” to “I don’t need it”. In that transition, other needs and ways of meeting them can take shape and acquire greater weight.

We can now answer the question posed at the beginning. The loss of appeal of that single prospect, remaining dependent on the agent and the circumstances of use, has not diminished the person’s freedom. What has fallen away is the confinement of the horizon to that single possibility. “I mustn’t” is still a form of the vortex, held in check from outside. “I don’t need it” belongs to a different, autonomous horizon.

I propose the image of an open spiral for this continuation of the neusis-horizon. A recognisable element of past experience returns in the imagination, whether it is the agent or the situation in which it was used. It now enters a different configuration of needs and relations. The former need to use and to remain dependent loses its force as a need, and something new can arise. If I no longer need this, perhaps I need something quite different. The spiral becomes a reshaping of the neusis-horizon over time. Meta-hairesis names the liminal state in the passage from “I mustn’t” to “I don’t need it,” in which other directions become available and can be held open to possible new images of oneself, and thus to a new purposiveness of existence.

For addiction as a redundantly stable system, a weakening of the cycle of dependence is destructive. The connections that constitute the addictive system can start to come apart. For the person suffering from addiction, the same process can enlarge the field of freedom if other ways of living open up. The breakdown of the addictive system opens the possibility of a new and healthier image of oneself. Here again it matters which organisation is breaking down and at what level other continuations become available.

This experience, attested in long-term psychotherapeutic treatment of severe addiction, lets us distinguish the self-reproduction of a causal trajectory in pathological states from an internal reconfiguration of relations. The latter can make other, constructive and non-pathological continuations available. They may remain open for quite some time to a new purposiveness.
9. Limits of the Account and Possible Objections

The ontological status of directions. The ontological status of co-present directions remains an open question. In this article I describe their availability in terms of a system’s organisation and its interaction with its environment. A stronger claim would concern the multiplicity of possible continuations of reality in its fullness and as a whole. That claim requires an argument of its own.

Does purposiveness become a hidden cause of choice? This may be the most serious objection. If purposiveness is the capacity of reality both to form a new image and to actualise it along an “optimal” vector, does it determine in advance which continuation will become actual? And does it thereby destroy the state we call freedom? Causal determinism would then simply give way to purposive determinism.

I think we can answer in the negative. As defined here, purposiveness lets us assess the direction in which a new whole is forming. The definition leaves open which structurally available direction will become actual, without positing an independent agency or force that determines it in advance. Purposiveness addresses what makes something genuinely new, while the question of what form it will take remains open. Here “optimality” refers to the most purposive departure, one that leaves room for a further expansion of the image of reality. The search for the best or most advantageous option among the available possibilities is a different undertaking. That room for further expansion is the neusis-horizon. Purposiveness thus sustains the openness of the horizon rather than closing it.

In earlier work, the image of a vector helped describe the optimal expansion of the image of reality in cognition [1, 2]. Whether this idea of directionality can be extended to reality as a whole also calls for separate consideration.

An aperture boundary for reality as a whole. For local systems, we can imagine and describe an aperture boundary. Can we speak of one for reality as such? That requires separate examination. The notions of a “boundary” and a “before” have highly specific meanings in physical cosmology, including in the Big Bang theory, so I would set those analogies aside here.

A methodological question. Can the distinction between purposiveness, the neusis-horizon, and meta-hairesis help us describe three different aspects of a transition in experience? These are (a) the formation of a new whole, (b) the availability of directions, and (c) the state in which they remain open. We would need criteria by which to recognise each aspect independently. Clinical experience with addiction offers some initial indications, and systematic investigation remains a task for future work.
10. Conclusion. Freedom as the Opening of the Possible
I propose that we regard purposiveness as reality’s inherent capacity to form a new image of itself. This ontological hypothesis grew out of earlier studies of cognition and has a wider scope.

A new image is a new whole in which the form and mode of existence of reality enter into a new relationship. A change may occur without a new image taking shape, and the loss of a local form can coincide with the continuation of a larger process of formation. Apoptosis offers an example. The programmed death of an individual cell may play a part in maintaining or reorganising a tissue or organism [16]. For the cell, this is the end of its existence. For the larger whole, it can be a condition of its proper organisation. The example shows that the assessment depends on scale. It does not, however, prove the universal purposiveness of nature.

Freedom can arise locally when several structurally available directions in which a new image could form open up within a causal process and can be held open by the system. I call this liminal state meta-hairesis. The metaphor of the aperture marks the boundary at which they open up, and the neusis-horizon describes the structure of the co-present directions. Choice may come later, when some of those directions take the form of definite options and one becomes actual.

Let us now return to the dilemma with which we began. Either the choice is determined and there is no freedom, or it is undetermined by causes and freedom becomes indistinguishable from chance. The proposed approach does not resolve the dilemma at the level of choice; it suggests that freedom should be sought elsewhere, in the state that can precede choice.

Freedom is the state in which a horizon of directions is held open for a system. The event of choosing may come later. Causality operates in this state, while the directions available to the system reach beyond the description of any one given trajectory. What eventually becomes actual grows out of a structured horizon of the possible. Whether the complete prior state of reality uniquely determines a new way for it to unfold then becomes a separate, open question.
The measure of freedom can provisionally be described in terms of the breadth and durability of openness, and, more conjecturally, the capacity to reshape the horizon of the possible itself.
The causal vortex and the open spiral describe two patterns of repetition. In the vortex, effects recreate the conditions for the same trajectory and narrow the horizon.

In the open spiral, a recognisable element of prior experience enters into new connections, which may open up other continuations. Causal continuity is maintained in both cases. The measure of freedom depends on which directions remain effectively available to the system and how their availability can change.
This gives us a concise definition.
Freedom is a state of meta-hairesis in which the neusis-horizon for forming a new, purposive image of reality opens and is held open.

In this definition, to repeat, purposiveness expresses the capacity of reality to form a new image of itself. Freedom concerns a state in time and space in which the directions in which a new image may take shape remain open to their subsequent purposive actualisation.

When the person says, “I don’t need it,” what they have gained goes beyond an additional choice. They have gained a horizon in which the old choice has lost its hold and new directions have become available.
Choice may be one of the consequences of freedom, without being its defining condition.
Perhaps the discussion of freedom itself should remain a spiral with an open aperture, rather than turn into a vortex of redundant stability in our own convictions.
